title: Κόραξ νοσῶν
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 168. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κόραξ νοσῶν ἔφη τῇ μητρί· « Μῆτερ, εὔχου τῷ θεῷ καὶ μὴ θρήνει. »
sentences.tr: Korax nosōn ephē tēi mētri· « Mēter, euchou tōi theōi kai mē thrēnei. »
sentences.l: A raven, being sick, said to his mother: « Mother, pray to the god and do not lament. »
sentences.n: εὔχου and θρήνει are present imperatives, and μή with the present imperative forbids something already going on — "leave off lamenting" rather than "do not begin". The god prayed to stands in the dative, τῷ θεῷ; which god is left open, and the mother's answer will make the vagueness the point.

sentences.t: Ἡ δ’ ὑπολαβοῦσα ἔφη· « Τίς σε, ὦ τέκνον, τῶν θεῶν ἐλεήσει ; τίνος γὰρ κρέας ὑπὸ σοῦ γε οὐκ ἐκλάπη ; »
sentences.tr: Hē d’ hypolabousa ephē· « Tis se, ō teknon, tōn theōn eleēsei ; tinos gar kreas hypo sou ge ouk eklapē ; »
sentences.l: And she, taking-up-the-word, said: « Which of the gods, my child, will pity you? For whose meat has not been stolen by you? »
sentences.i: And she answered: « Which of the gods, child, is going to pity you? Whose meat have you not stolen? »
sentences.n: ὑπολαβοῦσα is the regular verb of taking up another's words to reply, not of physical seizing. τίνος picks up τῶν θεῶν from the question before it — "which god's meat". Carrion birds were proverbial for making off with the flesh set out at sacrifices, and the mother's point is that her son has robbed every god there is, so that none is left to pity him. ἐκλάπη is the aorist passive of κλέπτω, and γε sharpens ὑπὸ σοῦ, "by you of all creatures". Chambry sets a space before the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ πολλοὺς ἐχθροὺς ἐν βίῳ ἔχοντες οὐδένα φίλον ἐν ἀνάγκῃ εὑρήσουσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti hoi pollous echthrous en biōi echontes oudena philon en anankēi heurēsousin.
sentences.l: The fable shows that those having many enemies in life will find not one friend in time of need.
sentences.n: οἱ … ἔχοντες is an articular participle, the standard Greek way of naming a class — "the ones who have" — and it is the usual subject of these morals. ἀνάγκη is constraint or compulsion, hence the pinch of necessity: distress, straits.
